name: Plum Purple
lede: Plum Purple is a dark, blue-leaning violet whose name was fixed by the painter Patrick Syme, who in 1814 moved Werner's plum blue into a new purple category.

sections.title: A mineralogist's purple
sections.body:
Plum Purple was a color of rocks and fruit before it was a color of paint [2][4]. In the mineralogical system of Abraham Werner it was filed as *plum blue*, one of the blues, between violet blue and lavender blue [4]. Patrick Syme's color book of 1814 made purple and orange principal colors, and the names beneath them moved with them: violet blue became [[violet-purple]], and plum blue became plum purple [1].

In Syme's table the color is number 42 [2]. His example from plants is the plum, and his example from minerals is fluor spar, the stone now called fluorite [2]. Baty reads number 42 as most likely descended from Jameson's Plum Blue, and notes that the 1821 edition of Syme carried it [2]. The neighboring purples were named from flowers, among them [[auricula-purple]], [[campanula-purple]], [[imperial-purple]] and [[pansy-purple]] [4].

sections.title: Syme's recipe
sections.body:
Syme did not leave the name to the eye alone. His text gives it as Berlin blue with a good deal of carmine red, a trace of brown and the faintest touch of black [3]. The recipe makes it a mixture of a blue and a red lake: [[berlin-blue]] and [[carmine]] carry the hue, and the brown and black only quiet it [3].

The next purple is built on this one. Auricula Purple, number 41, starts from this color and adds indigo blue and a good deal more carmine [3]. In Syme's system a color is therefore both a neighbor and a starting point, and the second edition grew to 110 references [1].

sections.title: Where Syme found it
sections.body:
Baty's plates show the color in three places that Syme's readers could check against the table [3]. It appears on the skin of a plum in an 1856 horticultural journal, on a fluorite specimen in Rashleigh's *Specimens of British Minerals* of 1797, and on the wing feathers of the spectacled cormorant in a zoological report of 1843 [3]. A fruit, a stone and a bird's wing share one dark, bluish plum tone.

The same words crossed into medicine. In 1827 the Nuremberg dermatologist Heinrich Eichhorn listed the colors seen in skin disease, among them a purple of a campanula, imperial or plum shade, three names that are all on Syme's list of purples [5][4]. A color table, he wrote, would be of great worth for judging skin illness [5].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
The swatch here is #463759 [6]. It is dark and quiet: lightness 26, chroma 23 and a hue angle of 309, which is blue-violet [6]. Against white it has a contrast ratio of about 10.8, so white lettering reads well on it (computed from the hex) [6].

It is much darker and bluer than the modern [[plum]], #8E4585, from which it sits roughly 30 units away in CIELAB (our own calculation) [6]. Its close neighbors are other old purples. [[violet-purple]] (#3A2F52, Syme's next name) and [[blackish-violet]] (#473B63, from Ridgway's 1912 atlas) are each within about 4 units of it [6].

Two similar names point elsewhere. The xkcd color survey gave a plum purple of #4E0550, a deeper and more saturated violet [6]. The Japanese *umemurasaki*, glossed "plum purple," is a reddish wine tone, #8F4155, filed here under [[light-wine]] [6].

sections.title: Books and records disagree on the date
sections.body:
The library records the color in three ways. Werner's nomenclature, in Syme's edition of 1821, is its earliest source in our data [6]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary of 1930 gives a first record of 1814, the year of Syme's first edition, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the swatch in block 212 [6]. Baty puts the descent of number 42 in the 1821 edition, from Jameson's Plum Blue, not in 1814 [2]. Which edition first printed the name *plum purple* is therefore not settled by these sources.

In printed English, the phrase reaches 5 per cent of its eventual peak by 1812 and peaks in the 1920s (Google Books, all senses, so plum fruit and purple can both inflate it) [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color match to this swatch turns up in 23 paintings, about 0.1 per cent, and in 12 when we count only paintings where it covers at least 5 per cent of the canvas (as photographed) [7]. It is rarer than 66 per cent of named colors in the archive [7].

The strongest matches are canvases dominated by it. Bronzino's [[painting:commons-Q48814933|Portrait of a girl]], from about 1545, is 40 per cent this color, and a portrait of Fiodor Alexeyevich Romanov from 1825 is 37 per cent [7]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 42 per cent of the 12 paintings, found by lightness rank within each painting [7].

The earliest dated match is 1539, in Sebastiano del Piombo's *La Piedad*, which is 282 years before the name's earliest record in our sources; it is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of a pigment [7]. The 1900s decade shows 6.7 times the expected rate (5 paintings of 809) [7]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test.
